senses.gloss:
Navagrahas
(‘nine प्लनेत्स्’)
------------------------------------------
For thousands of years, people all over the world have believed in the influence of the प्लनेत्स् on human life and history. Logically speaking, the च्रेअतिओन् of the प्लनेत्स् precedes that of the living beings. Hence, some sort of cause and effect relation must subsist between these two. This seems to be the basis for this belief.
The नवग्रहस् or the nine प्लनेत्स् are regarded by the Hindus as of the greatest astrological significance and are believed to influence the life of the individual as also the course of history.
As per the traditional list, the nine प्लनेत्स् are Ravi or सूर्य (sun), सोम or चन्द्र (moon), मङ्गल, कुज or अङ्गारक (Mars), बुध (Mercury), बृहस्पति or गुरु (Jupiter), शुक्र (Venus), शनि (Saturn), राहु and केतु. The seven days of the week have derived their names from the first seven प्लनेत्स्. राहु and केतु are not प्लनेत्स् but ascending and descending nodes of the मोओन्. Sometimes केतु is depicted as the personification of comets and meteors.
Śani, राहु and केतु are considered inauspicious, even positively maleficent, and responsible for children’s diseases. Hence they need to be propitiated.
The nine प्लनेत्स् are invariably found in every Śaiva temple in South India. In many North Indian temples they are depic-ted on the lintels of doors, to protect the temple and all those who enter it. They may also be housed in a separate मण्डप (a small pavilion) or at least a platform where the images of these nine ग्रहस् are installed in such a way that no two of them will face each other. It is sometimes stated that the images of the प्लनेत्स् are set up in the temples in the order in which they are in zodiacal circle at the time of construction of the temple.
The image of सूर्य must always be placed in the centre of the प्लनेत्स्, facing east, with the other ग्रहस् fixed round him, each in a specified direction. He has two hands, holding a lotus in each. His chariot has one wheel, is drawn by seven horses and has अरुण (deity of the dawn) as the charioteer.
Soma or चन्द्र has only a face and two hands but no body. He is shown holding white lotuses in his two hands. He rides on a two or three wheeled chariot drawn by ten horses.
Maṅgala or कुज has four hands, carrying the weapons mace and javelin in two, showing the varada and abhaya mudrās with the other two. He rides on a ram.
Budha also has four hands, three of them wielding the weapons sword, shield and mace. The last hand shows the varadamudrā. He rides on a lion or a chariot drawn by four horses.
Bṛhaspati being the गुरु, is shown holding a book and a rosary in his two hands. His chariot is golden and is driven by eight horses.
Śukra is also seated in a golden chariot drawn by eight horses or in a silver one drawn by ten horses. He has two hands holding a nidhi (= treasure) and a book. Sometimes he is shown with four hands holding the staff, rosary and water-pot, the fourth exhibiting the varadamudrā.
Śani rides in an iron chariot drawn by eight horses. He is more often shown as riding on a vulture. A buffalo also may be his mount. He holds the arrow, bow and javelin in three of his hands, the last hand being in the varadamudrā.
Rāhu is usually described as having only a face and केतु is depicted like a serpent’s tail. Iconographical works, however, describe them differently.
Rāhu may be shown riding a black lion or as seated on a सिṁहासन (throne) or in a silver chariot drawn by eight horses. He may have two hands, the right hand carrying a woollen blanket and a book, the left hand being shown empty. If four hands are shown, they carry sword, shield and lance, the fourth one being in varadamudrā.
Ketu has an ugly face and rides on a vulture. In his two arms he exhibits a mace and the varadamudrā or abhayamudrā.
All the ग्रहस् have crowns and ear-rings. The eight ग्रहस् round the Sun always face him.
The प्लनेत्स् are sometimes described as having connection with the इन्चर्नतिओन् of Lord विष्णु.

navānna
(‘[ceremony of offering] cooked rice [from] the new crop’)
------------------------------------------
Every act in a Hindu’s life is, somehow or the other, to be connected with God and religion. The ‘navānna’ is one such.
When paddy is harvested, the rice got out of it should first be offered to God and living beings before using it. This ceremony of offering cooked rice is called ‘navānna’ and is generally done in the month of Agrahāyaṇa or Mārgaśira (December-January). Performance of śrāddhas and feeding birds and animals are a part of this.
See also ĀGRAYAṆA and MAKARA-SAṄKRĀNTI.

Navagva
(‘those who have completed it in nine [months]’)
------------------------------------------
One of the सप्तर्षिस् or the Seven Sages is अङ्गिरस्. Among the descendants of Aṅgiras—known as Āṅgirasas—those who performed a सत्त्रयाग (which normally needs twelve months to complete) and attained what they wanted in nine months were called ‘Navagvas’ and those who got the results in ten months, were called ‘Daśagvas’ (vide Ṛgveda 1.62.4).
Sometimes the Navagvas and the Daśagvas themselves are identified with the सप्तर्षिस्.
They are supposed to live in the पितृलोक (world of manes) and accept the obsequial offerings.

Navyanyāya
------------------------------------------
The न्याय दर्शन or the न्याय school of Hindu philosophy has provided a strong basis and framework for Hindu लोगिच्.
A new school of न्याय philosophy under the name ‘Navyanyāya’ began with the writings of गङ्गेश उपाध्याय (A. D. 1200) of मिथिला (in Bihar) and his successors. He wrote a work called Tattva-cintāmaṇi wherein he has dwelt with only the four प्रमाणस् or means of knowledge, viz., प्रत्यक्ष (direct perception), anu-māna (inference), उपमान (comparison) and शब्द (verbal testimony). He did not touch the prameya (objects to be known) at all.
Somehow this work of his attracted an unusually great attention of the scholars, first at मिथिला and later at नवद्वीप of Bengal.
Raghunātha Śiromaṇi (A. D. 1500), मथुरा Bhaṭṭācārya (A. D. 1580), गदा-dhara Bhaṭṭācārya (A. D. 1650) and Jaga-dīśa Bhaṭṭācārya (A. D. 1590) were the chief commentators of this work of गङ्गेश.
Later on, several sub-commentaries on the commentary of Raghunātha Śiromaṇi arose, along with independent works on the same object, thus enriching the Navya-न्याय literature.
The contribution of Navya-न्याय was mainly in the direction of developing a system of linguistic notations to specify accurately and precisely, any concept. The other aspects of न्याय दर्शन were practically untouched.
See also GAṄGEŚA.

Navadvīpa
(‘the new island’)
------------------------------------------
This was the birthplace of श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य (A. D. 1486-1533) considered as a combined इन्चर्नतिओन् of राधा and कृष्ण. He was the founder and pioneer of Beṅgāl वैष्णविस्म्.
Navadvīpa has been identified with the modern Nadia. It is a small town situated on the bank of the river भागीरथी (Gaṅgā) at its confluence with the river Jalāṅgī.
It was a prominent seat of learning during the period A. D. 1198 to 1757, and produced many eminent logicians like Raghunātha, Śiromaṇi and others.
It was the capital of the kings of Sen dynasty.

Navagrahaśāntis
(‘appeasement rites for the nine प्लनेत्स्’)
------------------------------------------
That the various प्लनेत्स् circling round the sun in our solar system, have an effect on the lives of the living beings here, is a belief shared by many peoples of this earth, throughout the history of mankind. A holistic approach, engendered by holistic sciences, is also lending credence to such beliefs.
The Hindu scriptures have recognised this factor since the most ancient times. If and when a particular planet is unfavourably placed, as indicated by the होरोस्चोपे of the person, certain religious rites known as ‘śāntis’ have to be performed, to offset, or at least minimise, these effects. Out of these, the Navagrahaśānti—also called ‘Navagraha-makha’—is also one and has been considered as a प्रकृति or a model for other types of शान्तिस्.
Sometimes the Navagrahaśānti, identified with नवग्रहमख, is said to be of three types: ayutahoma, लक्षहोम and कोटिहोम, wherein the oblations into the duly consecrated fire are ten thousand, one lakh and one crore.
The Navagrahaśānti should be offered to the image of the nine प्लनेत्स् made out of nine different kinds of materials (like copper, crystal, red sandalwood etc.) or to the pictures of the nine प्लनेत्स् drawn with sandalwood paste on a piece of cloth. The mantras used in the rites are usually from the वेदस् (e.g., Ṛgveda 1.35.2; Vājasaneyī Saṁhitā 9.40; Taittirīya Saṁhitā 4.7.13.5).
Homa to each planet is done with समिध् (fuel sticks) anointed with honey or ghee, the number being 108, or 28. The ब्राह्मण priests performing the śānti must be suitably rewarded.
Special gifts are to be made when any planet is unfavourably placed. The Navagrahaśānti itself can be performed at the beginning of all auspicious or important occasions like the सṁस्कारस् (sacraments), going on a पिल्ग्रिमगे, before a battle and so on.

Navarātra
(‘[festival of] nine nights’)
------------------------------------------
‘Navarātra’ means a period of nine nights, or for that matter, a period of nine days. Two Navarātras are mentioned in the पुराणस् and the धर्मशास्त्रस्, as being highly auspicious for the worship of शक्ति or the Divine मोथेर् दुर्गा. They are: Vasantanavarātra, the first nine days in the Vasanta ṛtu or spring, from चैत्र śukla pratipad up to navamī; Śarannavarātra, the first nine days in the Śaradṛtu or autumn, from Āśvayuja śukla pratipad to navamī. However, in practice, the celebration of the former has yielded its place almost completely to the latter.
Though this नवरात्र is celebrated all over the country in some form or the other, it is the दुर्गोत्सव or the festival of मोथेर् दुर्गा that steals the show.
Celebration of the नवरात्र festival varies from place to place in other parts of the country. In South India, goddess सरस्वती is worshipped on the saptamī day and दुर्गा on the aṣṭamī. The worship is done in the picture and not in clay images as in Bengal. The navamī day, called ‘Mahānavamī’, is celebrated as Āyudhapūjā, the instruments and implements that help us to earn our livelihood being worshipped then. This is akin to the Viśvakarmapūjā performed in the North, during the month of Bhādrapada when Ravi (the Sun) enters the zodiacal sign of कन्या (Virgo). In almost all the homes, there will be display of dolls with decorations. This is a special attraction for children.
In several parts of North India, especially in the Hindi belt, नवरात्र is celebrated as रामलीला. Recitations from the Rāmāyaṇa, enacting plays based on the several episodes of the epic and processions culminating in the burning of the effigies of रावण, कुम्भकर्ण and मेघनाद on the daśamī day (also called विजयदशमी) are the salient features of these celebrations.
In the Mysore City of Karnataka, the Dasara festival celebrated during the नवरात्र, has been very famous. It was a royal festival celebrated by the Mahārājā (King) of Mysore, ending with a grand procession on the विजयदशमी day.
Now-a-days, an image of Cāmuṇ-ḍeśvarī (an aspect of दुर्गा) is taken out in procession.

Navadurgās
(‘the nine Durgās’)
------------------------------------------
Durgā is one of the most popular and widely worshipped aspects of the Divine मोथेर्, पार्वती. She is—according to the famous work Devīmāhātmya—the personification of the essence and powers of all the gods.
Works on the देवी-cult sometimes put forward several varieties of दुर्गा. Nine of these are often grouped together and called ‘Navadurgās’.
According to the Kavacastotra of the Devīmāhātmya, they are: Śailaputrī, ब्रह्मचारिणी, Candraghaṇṭā, Kūṣmāṇḍā, Skandamātā, कात्यायनी, Kālarātrī, Mahā-गौरी and Siddhidātrī.
As per the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa, the list includes: Nīlakaṇṭhī, क्षेमङ्करी, Harasiddhi, वनदुर्गा, Rudradurgā, Agnidurgā, Jayadurgā, Vindhyavāsinī and Ripumāridurgā.
Iconographically, the main deity is shown with 18 arms (or hands) and the other eight with 16 hands. The various objects shown in the hands are more or less the same as those of the main goddess. Some of them are: अक्षमाला (rosary), खेटक (shield), खड्ग (sword), दर्पण (mirror), धनुस् (bow), बाण (arrow), ध्वज (banner), tarjanī-मुद्रा (pose of warning), शक्ति (spear), mudgara (hatchet), śūla (lance), चक्र (discus), शङ्ख (conch) and so on.
These different aspects may be invoked for different purposes.
See also DEVĪMĀHĀTMYA and DURGĀ.

Navārṇamantra
(‘mantra of nine letters’)
------------------------------------------
The Devīmāhātmya, also known as the Durgāsaptaśatī and the Caṇḍī, is a pre-eminent work of the Śāktatantras or the देवी-cult. (See DEVĪMĀHĀTMYA for details.) This whole work of 700 verses is considered as a powerful मन्त्र with specific rules prescribed for its recitation, by which one can get whatever result one wants.
One of the most important part of its recitation is the repitition of the Navārṇamantra—also called Navākṣarī—since it has nava or nine arṇas or syllables.
The मन्त्र is: aiṁ ह्रीṁ klīṁ cāmuṇḍāyai vicce.
The first three syllables represent Mahāsarasvatī, महालक्ष्मी and Mahākālī, the three main aspects of the Divine मोथेर्, दुर्गा. They also represent the three states of Sat (eternal existence), Cit (eternal चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्) and आनन्द (eternal bliss).
The word ‘vicce’ consists of three parts: vit, ca, e. They represent our physical, vital and mental states.
‘Cāmuṇḍāyai’ means to ‘Cāmuṇḍā’.
The total meaning of the मन्त्र is ‘By the grace of the मोथेर् चामुण्डा, we are freed from the present condition of physical, vital and mental states, and raised to the highest state of Sat-cit-आनन्द.’
The word ‘Varṇa’ for letter, also means ‘colour’. It is said that mantras have their own spectrums which can be perceived in inner contemplation. Hence each letter of this मन्त्र has to be contemplated in a definite colour. They are:
aim moon-like lustre.
hrīm effulgence of the sun.
klīm blazing fire.
cā shining golden colour.
muṇ deep red.
ḍā deep blue.
yai black.
vi white.
cce smoky hue.

The जप of the Navārṇamantra is always done as a part of the recitation of the Durgāsaptaśatī, though rarely, it can be done independently also.

Navagrahamakha
------------------------------------------
This is the same as Navagrahaśānti.
See NAVAGRAHAŚĀNTIS for details.
